topic: Open & closed innovation, distributed innovation I

questions.stem: Who developed the open innovation framework?
questions.explanation: Henry Chesbrough introduced the open innovation framework in his 2003 book of the same name.

questions.stem: An 'outside-in' (inbound) open-innovation flow involves:
choices: Licensing internally developed IP to a competitor.
Bringing external knowledge, IP, or technology into the firm.
Donating patents to a standards body.
Spinning out an internal project as an independent company.
questions.explanation: Outside-in (inbound) flows bring external knowledge in: licensing in, university partnerships, acquisitions, crowdsourcing.

questions.stem: An 'inside-out' (outbound) open-innovation flow involves:
choices: Taking internally developed knowledge to market through external channels — licensing out, spin-outs, open-sourcing.
Hiring senior researchers from a competitor.
questions.explanation: Inside-out flows monetise or release internal IP to external channels: licensing out, spin-outs, open-source contributions, donations to standards bodies.

questions.stem: Procter & Gamble's 'Connect + Develop' programme is the canonical example of:
questions.explanation: P&G C+D targets ~50% of innovation from external sources via crowdsourcing, university links, and supplier partnerships — textbook outside-in.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of Chesbrough's reasons closed innovation eroded?
choices: Increased labour mobility of skilled engineers
Growth of venture capital enabling employee defections
questions.explanation: University research has grown, not declined. The classical erosion forces include labour mobility, VC, external suppliers, shorter cycles, and distributed knowledge.

questions.stem: Xerox PARC is a frequently cited example of:
choices: Closed innovation that generated breakthrough inventions but failed to commercialise many of them.
questions.explanation: PARC invented the GUI, ethernet, mouse, and laser printing. Xerox commercialised laser printing well but let the others escape via spin-outs (Adobe, 3Com).

questions.stem: Google open-sourcing Kubernetes is best understood as:
choices: An inside-out flow with the strategic logic of commoditising a complement to capture value elsewhere (cloud).
questions.explanation: Open-sourcing Kubernetes commoditised container orchestration, driving cloud adoption where Google captured value via GCP. Classic 'commoditise your complement'.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of the COUPLED mode of open innovation?
choices: Licensing a patent in from a university
Spinning out a research project as a startup
questions.explanation: Coupled mode = joint creation with partners. SEMATECH (US semiconductor consortium), JVs, and standards bodies are canonical examples.

questions.stem: A defensive patent portfolio is held primarily to:
choices: Deter litigation by other patent holders (mutual assured destruction / cross-licensing)
questions.explanation: Defensive portfolios deter rather than monetise: a competitor who sues will be countersued. Microsoft, Google, and Apple all hold large defensive portfolios.

questions.stem: Which assumption belongs to the CLOSED innovation paradigm?
choices: Useful ideas are widely distributed; we should tap external sources.
If we get to market first, we win — therefore IP must be tightly controlled.
Spinning out unused IP can create new revenue.
Crowdsourcing can outperform internal R&D for some problems.
questions.explanation: First-mover plus tight IP control is a classical closed-innovation tenet. The others are open-innovation positions.

questions.stem: Lego Ideas, where customers submit designs and earn royalties, is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Customer co-creation is an outside-in mechanism. Lego Ideas pulls external (user) innovation into the firm.

questions.stem: Which company is the canonical example of monetising an inside-out licensing strategy?
questions.explanation: IBM earns substantial revenue per year licensing out its patent portfolio — the textbook inside-out monetisation case.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a typical risk of open innovation?
choices: Giving away core IP that weakens competitive position
Loss of strategic focus across too many partners
questions.explanation: Open innovation does not reduce patent-filing ability. It increases strategic, IP-leak, and governance risks.

questions.stem: Chesbrough argues that the boundary of the firm should be:
choices: Fully open with all IP shared.
Porous and actively managed, with flows in both directions selected per technology and stage.
questions.explanation: Open innovation is a portfolio decision: porous, actively managed, asymmetric per technology and per business unit.

questions.stem: A 'patent thicket' refers to:
choices: An area with many overlapping patents that complicate product development without cross-licensing or pools.
questions.explanation: Patent thickets (e.g. mobile phone radios, MPEG video) are navigated via cross-licensing or patent pools like MPEG-LA.

questions.stem: Pharma firms commonly license molecules in from biotechs and universities. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Licensing in external IP is the textbook outside-in flow. Pharma is one of the most open-innovative industries by this measure.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of an inside-out STANDARDS contribution?
choices: Donating IP to a standards body (e.g. W3C, IETF) to grow an open standard and the market around it.
questions.explanation: Donating IP to standards bodies is an inside-out move with strategic value: an open standard expands the market, in which the donor competes from a strong position.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument FOR open innovation in fast-moving industries?
choices: Closed pipelines are too slow; external knowledge accelerates time-to-market and shares risk.
questions.explanation: Speed and risk-sharing are core open-innovation benefits in industries with short product lifecycles.

questions.stem: Which research lab is the canonical 20th-century closed-innovation exemplar that produced the transistor and information theory?
questions.explanation: Bell Labs (under AT&T) is the textbook closed-innovation case: transistor, laser, information theory, UNIX, C — all internally developed.

questions.stem: A spin-out is an inside-out mechanism in which:
choices: The firm sells a subsidiary to a competitor.
An internal project is launched as an independent company, often with the parent retaining equity.
questions.explanation: Spin-outs let unused or non-core IP commercialise without distorting the parent's core focus. Xerox produced many famous (and lucrative) spin-outs.

questions.stem: Open innovation does NOT mean:
choices: Actively managing the firm boundary for flows in both directions.
Giving away all proprietary IP for free.
Combining internal R&D with external knowledge.
Licensing in and licensing out as strategic choices.
questions.explanation: A common misconception. Open innovation is about managed openness, not blanket disclosure. Core IP often stays closed.

questions.stem: Which is the cleanest one-line difference between closed and open innovation?
choices: Closed uses patents; open does not.
Closed assumes the smart people work for us; open assumes useful knowledge is widely distributed and the boundary should be porous.
Closed is American; open is European.
questions.explanation: Chesbrough's most-quoted contrast is the assumption about where smart people are. Everything else follows from that.

questions.stem: Why might a firm OPEN-SOURCE a non-core technology?
choices: To commoditise a complement so that demand for the firm's core product grows.
questions.explanation: Commoditising a complement is a classical strategic move. Google's Android open-sourcing grew mobile internet, in which Google captured ad revenue.

questions.stem: A pharma firm licenses an early-stage molecule from a university and runs Phase II via a contract research organisation. The flow structure is best described as:
choices: Outside-in from the university; CRO partnership is typically outside-in (service procurement) rather than coupled.
questions.explanation: The molecule license is clearly outside-in. CRO is a paid service relationship, more outside-in than coupled (no joint IP creation). Coupled mode requires shared IP creation.

questions.stem: Which statement about open innovation is MOST accurate?
choices: Open innovation always outperforms closed innovation empirically.
Open innovation is a portfolio decision per technology, per business unit, per stage — not a binary stance.
Open innovation is incompatible with patenting.
Open innovation is only relevant for software firms.
questions.explanation: The exam-correct view: open vs closed is a per-decision portfolio choice. Some IP stays closed, some opens, some flows in, some flows out — the CEO manages the mix.
